sections.body: This section looks at ten creative disciplines and what artificial intelligence is doing inside each one right now. In visual art, models turn text prompts into finished illustrations, and artists use them for concept work, editorial images and print. In film and video, synthesis tools generate shots, extend footage and build backgrounds that would once have needed a full set. Musicians use AI for stems, mixing and mastering, and singers license synthetic voices for recordings and live shows. Choreographers map motion capture onto avatars, writers draft and revise with language models, and photographers use generative tools for retouching and compositing. The work is real and shipping, not a demo.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The tools are good at producing plausible output fast, and that is where most of the solved ground sits. What is not solved is authorship, credit and payment, and the legal picture is unsettled: this site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, 18 of them involving AI music services. Quality is uneven across disciplines, with still images ahead of long-form video and voice, and control over a specific result still takes iteration and craft. Provenance is partial, since watermarks and metadata can be stripped or ignored. The honest limit is that generation is cheap and judgment is not, so the value keeps landing on the people who can direct, select and finish.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages run from the most mature disciplines to the most contested. Visual Arts and Generative Illustration and Photography and Hyper-Realism cover still images, one from the drawing side and one from the camera side, and both lean on the 1000 live image generation models this site tracks. Cinematography and Video Synthesis and Choreography and Motion Mapping handle moving pictures, with the 1000 video models behind the first and motion capture behind the second. Vocal Synthesis and Operatic Performance and Music Composition and Audio Engineering split voice from composition, drawing on the 2000 audio models and the music lawsuits. Literary Arts and Narrative Design and Theater and Virtual Set Design cover text and staged space, while Interactive and Experiential Art covers installation and audience-facing work. Rights and Provenance in AI Art is the closing page and the one to read first if ownership is the question, since it gathers the licensing, watermarking and lawsuit material that the other nine pages keep running into.
